p: The ancient Greeks told that fire was stolen from the gods by the Titan Prometheus, who carried it down to mankind hidden in the hollow stalk of a fennel plant, and that he was punished for it by being chained to a rock, where an eagle ate his liver every day, and every night it grew again. It is a story of extraordinary cruelty and extraordinary insight. The Greeks understood that fire was the gift which divided men from beasts, and they suspected that it had been dearly bought.

No animal but man makes fire, or keeps it, or carries it from place to place. Chimpanzees, the Encyclopaedia tells me, have been observed to watch wild fires with calm attention and to forage in the burnt ground afterwards; that is as far as they go. At some point in the immense past, one of our ancestors went further, and fed the flame instead of fleeing it.

The question of when is one of the most disputed in the whole study of our origins, and I must give you the dispute honestly. Fire leaves traces, ashes and burnt bone and reddened earth, but wild fires leave the same traces, and the difficulty is to distinguish a hearth from a lightning strike. The Encyclopaedia reports burnt material in association with early human remains in Africa from as long ago as one and a half million years, at places in Kenya called Koobi Fora and Chesowanja, but these are contested. Firmer evidence comes from a cave in South Africa called Wonderwerk, meaning wonder work in the Afrikaans tongue, where burnt bone and ash of about one million years ago were found deep inside the cave, where no wild fire could have reached. In the Near East, at a site in Israel called Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, there is good evidence of repeated burning of about eight hundred thousand years ago. By about four hundred thousand years ago, hearths become common in the record, and in the later ages of the Neanderthals and of our own kind, fire was everywhere.

Whether those first fire-users could make fire, or could only keep a flame taken from a burning tree, is another matter. To keep fire is a constant labour; it must be fed and sheltered and carried in embers when the band moves on. To make it, by striking flint upon a stone containing iron, or by spinning a stick of wood rapidly against another until the dust smoulders, is a later and more difficult art. The Encyclopaedia admits that we do not know when it was first mastered. I suspect that for a very long time, the loss of a fire was a calamity, and the keeping of it a sacred duty. Something of that feeling survives in the eternal flame of the Vestal Virgins of Rome, who were buried alive if they let it go out, and perhaps, more mildly, in the reproach that Mrs Pruett delivers to the maid when the kitchen range is allowed to die.

Consider first warmth. With fire, our ancestors could live in colder lands, and survive the long winters of the Ice Ages in Europe and northern Asia. Consider next light. The day of a creature without fire ends at sunset; the day of a creature with fire is lengthened by some hours, and those hours are not spent hunting or gathering, for that is impossible in the dark, but sitting together. It is not fanciful to suppose that the first long conversations of mankind, the first stories, the first teaching of the young, took place around the hearth. Consider protection: the great cats, wolves and bears of the ancient world feared fire, and a band with a fire at the mouth of its cave slept more securely. Consider tools: wood hardened in the flame makes a better spear point, and certain stones, gently heated, flake more cleanly.

But the greatest gift was cooking. A learned man of the future, Professor Richard Wrangham of Harvard College in America, has argued at length that cooking made us human. Cooked food is softer and yields more of its nourishment with less chewing and less digestion. Raw, a great many roots and meats are tough, and some are poisonous; cooked, they are wholesome. Professor Wrangham observes that our teeth, jaws and bellies are small for an ape of our size, and our brains, which consume a great deal of nourishment, very large; and he proposes that cooking paid for the brain. Other scholars think he places cooking too early. I cannot judge between them. But I find it entirely plausible that the kitchen, that most despised of rooms in a gentleman's house, is the true birthplace of the human mind.

The hearth is also a social invention, and here the historian may speak with more confidence. A fire must be tended. Someone must gather wood, someone watch the flame, someone carry the embers on the march. Food cooked over a shared fire must be shared, and sharing requires rules: who eats first, who gets the best portion, who goes without. In the great majority of human societies that we know, the hearth is the centre of the household, and the household is the root of every larger order. The Latin word for hearth is focus, from which we take our word for the point at which things are gathered together. The Romans worshipped Vesta, goddess of the hearth, in every home, and the Greek name for the same goddess, Hestia, stood for the household itself.

There is a darker side, as there is to every human gift. Fire burns forests and cities. It was used in war from the earliest times we know. It was, in my own country, an instrument of religious persecution within the reign of Queen Mary. And the men of the future, I am informed, have learned to make fires in their engines on so prodigious a scale that the smoke of them is changing the very climate of the globe. Prometheus would not be surprised. The gods, he might say, were not wrong to fear what mankind would do with their gift. They were only wrong to think they could keep it from us.
